pairs.en: On the sixth of the month, the holy Church of God joyfully keeps the remembrance of the divine TRANSFIGURATION of our Lord and God and Saviour Jesus Christ.
*Tabor was glorified beyond every place on earth,* *for it saw the nature of God shining in glory.* *On the sixth, Christ changed his human form.*

The reason for this feast is as follows. Our Master Christ often forewarned his holy disciples about the dangers, the sufferings and the death he himself was to undergo, and about the slaughter and death that awaited his disciples too. But since the dangers and hardships were immediate, belonging to this present life, while the good things they were to receive lay beyond them and were only hoped for, the Lord wished, for this reason, to assure his disciples with their own eyes what that glory is, and what kind of glory it is, with which he will come at the general resurrection — the glory they too were to share.

So he took them up a high mountain, apart by themselves, and was transfigured before them: his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as light, and Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with Christ. He took with him only three of the Apostles, as the foremost and most eminent: Peter, because he loved Christ so dearly; John, because he was loved by Christ; and James, because he was able to drink the cup of death, which the Lord himself also drank.

He brought Moses and Elijah to stand among them, to correct the mistaken suspicions that many held about him — for some said the Lord was Elijah, and others that he was Jeremiah. For this reason, then, he set before them on Tabor the first and foremost of the prophets, so that the disciples might know, and through the disciples all people might know, how great a difference there is between Christ and the Prophets. For Christ is the Master, and the prophets are his servants; and so that they might learn that the Lord holds authority over death and over life, he brought Moses from among the dead, and Elijah from among the living. (See the treasury of Damascene, and Makarios the Deaf.)
To him be the glory and the dominion, unto the ages. Amen.

See, at the end of the present volume, a notable dissertation on when the Transfiguration took place, by the Archimandrite Sir Dorotheos Evelpides. This respected and learned friend, moved by zeal for the truth and yielding to our entreaties, has allowed it to be published in the present edition. — the 1868 editor

Since our subject here is the Transfiguration, we note, for the sake of scholars, when this feast actually took place. We say that, according to Eusebius of Caesarea (as reported by Koressios) and most of the teachers of the Church, the Transfiguration happened forty days before the Passion — the prose-writer of Damascus bears witness to this too, in his sermon on the Transfiguration — that is, it took place in the month of February, and not in August, as it is now kept. That this opinion is the more probable one, and the more widely held in the Church of Christ, is confirmed by what follows.

First: the Evangelist Matthew, who was an eyewitness and ear-witness disciple and apostle of the Lord, says that even before he was transfigured, the Lord was already saying this to his disciples: “From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised” (Matthew 16:21). From these words it follows that the Transfiguration took place close to the Passion.

Second: by the order and sequence of the chapters of the Evangelist Matthew, the Transfiguration took place near the Passion; for the same Matthew, having told of the divine Transfiguration in chapter 17, only three chapters later goes straight on to Palm Sunday, in chapter 21.

Third: the celebrated teacher Joseph Bryennios, too, says in his work *On Spring* (p. 48 of volume 3) that the Transfiguration took place close to the Passion, which occurred at the spring equinox, on the 23rd of March.
The Transfiguration, then, took place in February, but it was moved, and is kept, in August.

First, because the Transfiguration, having taken place, as we said, forty days before the Passion, would sometimes fall within Great Lent; and since it is a feast signifying the age to come, it needed to be kept for eight days running — and this was unfitting during the fast of holy Lent, a season of mourning that signifies this present life of hardship.

Second, it was moved to August, and to no other month, for this reason: see the wisdom and understanding of the divine Fathers who ordered these sacred matters so well. Since, as we said, the Transfiguration took place forty days before the Passion and the Cross, and the Exaltation of the precious Cross is kept on the 14th of September and stands for the Cross and the Passion of the Lord, the holy Fathers, counting forty days back from that day, ordained that the divine Transfiguration should be kept on the 6th of August — because from the 6th of August to the 14th of September come exactly forty whole days, no more and no less.

The same divine Fathers also ordained that at the feast of the Transfiguration the Katavasiai to be sung should not be the canon-odes of that same feast — as is usual at the other feasts of the Lord, such as the Nativity of Christ, the Meeting in the Temple, and the Theophany, where the Katavasiai are the odes of those same feasts — but instead ordained that the Katavasiai sung at it should be the odes of the Exaltation of the Cross, so as to show the connection which the Transfiguration has with the Passion, and the 6th of August with the 14th of September, that is, with the Exaltation of the Cross.
That is also why the very first troparion of the Transfiguration opens at once by pointing to the Cross, saying: “Before your Cross, O Lord...”

That none of this happened by chance or of itself, without care or design, but with careful attention, any sensible person will agree — for who can say it is by chance that exactly forty days are found from the 6th of August, on which the Transfiguration is kept, to the 14th of September, on which the Exaltation of the Cross is kept, no more and no less? Certainly no one.

I know that Meletios of Athens, in the first volume of his *Ecclesiastical History*, says that the Lord was transfigured on the 6th of August — but he ought to have brought some witness for his words, rather than tell us things with neither source nor witness: that Jesus was walking about in Galilee in the middle of April, that he left Galilee at the beginning of May, and on such-and-such a day of the month, and such-and-such a day of the week, did this miracle, and on another day, that one — a thing which not even an apostle and disciple of the Lord, an eyewitness and ear-witness of his miracles and words, could have set down with such fine detail and precision.
I am amazed, then, how anyone can believe things so entirely without witness or proof.

And if anyone objects with the payment of the didrachma, which Matthew mentions after the Transfiguration, saying it was paid in the month of Tishri, that is, in September, and concludes from this that the Transfiguration took place on the 6th of August, we answer that he does not speak rightly.

For while the royal and civil dues were collected in September, the beginning of the civil year, the didrachma, being a priestly due, was also collected in March, the beginning of the legal year, that is, by the Law of Moses.

That the didrachma was a priestly due, given to the priests, the divine Scripture testifies: “And Moses gave the redemption-money of those who were over the number — which were the didrachmas — to Aaron and his sons, at the word of the Lord, as the Lord commanded Moses” (Numbers 3:51).

And if anyone objects with the Evangelist Luke, that in the ninth chapter of his Gospel he places the Transfiguration and not later, we answer that this Evangelist customarily writes things out of their true order — that is, he writes later events earlier.

So too the hospitality shown him at Bethany, in the house of the Pharisee, that is, of Simon the leper, which actually happened later, he places earlier, as some judge (see also p. 51 of the newly printed Centenary); and almost immediately after coming down from the mountain of the forty days' fast, he writes that the Lord entered the synagogue and stood up to read — which took place in the second year of the Lord's preaching of the Gospel, according to the author of that same Centenary, Mr Evgenios (p. 43).
So too the Transfiguration, which he ought to have written among the later chapters of his Gospel, he wrote earlier.

One might wonder why, day after day, at every Hour, the Kontakion of the Transfiguration is said, and not that of some other feast. We answer: because this feast of the Transfiguration is a feast of the age to come — for just as the Apostles beheld the glory of Christ at the Transfiguration, so too the blessed will behold that same glory of Christ in the age to come, as Dionysius the Areopagite teaches in the first chapter of *On the Divine Names*.

For this reason the Church, wishing Christians always to keep that glory which they are to enjoy in their memory, ordained that its Kontakion should be said every day, so that by constant reminder it might stir in them longing and desire for that future glory.

For just as, to give an example, the judge of a contest, by showing the athlete the crown, gladdens his heart and strengthens him to compete lawfully and with endurance so as to win so fair and precious a crown, so too the Church of Christ, by setting before the Christian contestants of piety the crown of divine glory they are to enjoy, gladdens them and strengthens them to contend bravely, that they may be made worthy of so beautiful and fair a crown of unfading blessedness.

Note that Chrysostom composed four sermons on the feast of the Transfiguration: one beginning “Amen, Amen I say to you, that there are some”; another, “Come, lovers of the feast, today as well”; a third, “Since much is said concerning dangers”; and a fourth, “If anyone will hear you, O God-chosen assembly.”

John of Damascus, whose sermon begins “Come, let us keep festival today.” Andrew of Crete, whose begins “As many as rejoice in the self-emptying of the Word.” Gregory Palamas wrote two: one beginning “We too praise and marvel,” the other “Isaiah the Prophet, concerning the Gospel.” Ephraim the Syrian, whose begins “From the region the joy of summer.” Anastasios the Sinaite delivered a sermon on Mount Tabor itself, which begins “How awe-inspiring is this place — I too stand beside myself with wonder.” (The above are preserved in the Great Lavra, in the community of Dionysiou, and in the monasteries of Iveron and Pantokrator.)

Nikephoros Choumnos, keeper of the imperial inkstand (preserved at the Pantokrator monastery). Makarios Chrysokephalos, whose begins “God the Lord has appeared upon the mountain” (preserved in his own printed book). Canons in all eight tones on the Transfiguration are also found at the Pantokrator monastery, composed by Matthew of Karyes. Athanasios, Proklos and Antiochos also have sermons on the Transfiguration (in the newly printed Sacred Ritual); and at the Lavra a sermon of Timothy, presbyter of Antioch, is also kept, beginning “With many and various weapons.” As for the sermon above, attributed to Chrysostom, beginning “Come, lovers of the feast, today as well” — many hold that this one is in fact the work of Saint Proklos.
Through the prayers of your Saints, Christ our God, have mercy on us.
